lessons.title: Macronutrients: Protein
lessons.description: Protein structure, HBV vs LBV sources, complementation, and dietary alternatives.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Protein?

Protein is one of the three macronutrients. It is found in every cell of the body and is essential for growth, repair, and maintenance of tissues such as muscle, skin, hair, and nails. Protein also plays a role in making enzymes, hormones, and antibodies that keep the body functioning properly.

Protein is made up of building blocks called amino acids. There are 20 amino acids found in protein. The body can make some of these itself, but eight must come from the food we eat. These are called essential amino acids (EAAs): isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, and valine.

Key Fact

In young children, additional amino acids such as histidine and tyrosine are sometimes considered “conditionally essential” because their bodies cannot yet produce them in sufficient quantities.

Functions of Protein

Protein carries out several vital functions in the body. Understanding these is important for the exam because questions often ask you to explain why protein is needed.

Growth: Children, teenagers, and pregnant women need protein to build new cells and tissues as the body grows. Repair: When tissues are damaged — through injury, surgery, or everyday wear — protein provides the raw materials to rebuild them. Maintenance: Even in adults who are not growing, protein is needed to replace cells that die naturally, such as skin cells and red blood cells.

Secondary functions: Protein is also used to make enzymes (which speed up chemical reactions in the body), hormones (which carry chemical messages), and antibodies (which fight infection). In an emergency, when carbohydrate and fat stores are depleted, the body can use protein as a source of energy — providing 4 kcal per gram.

HBV and LBV Proteins

Not all protein sources are equal. The exam board distinguishes between two categories based on amino acid content.

HBV (high biological value) proteins contain all eight essential amino acids. Most animal sources are HBV: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk, cheese, and yoghurt. Soya is the only common plant source that is also HBV, which makes it particularly important for vegetarians and vegans.

LBV (low biological value) proteins are missing one or more essential amino acids. Most plant sources are LBV: pulses (beans, lentils, chickpeas), nuts, seeds, cereals (wheat, rice, oats), and vegetables. This does not mean LBV proteins are bad — it means people who rely on them need to combine different sources to get all eight EAAs.

Key Fact

HBV = all 8 EAAs (animal sources + soya). LBV = missing 1 or more EAAs (most plant sources). Remember: soya is the exception — it is a plant source but HBV.

Animal sources (HBV): Meat (beef, lamb, pork), poultry (chicken, turkey), fish (salmon, tuna, cod), eggs, milk, cheese, yoghurt.

Plant sources (mostly LBV): Pulses (lentils, kidney beans, chickpeas), nuts (almonds, cashews, peanuts), seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, chia), cereals (wheat, rice, oats), vegetables (peas, spinach, broccoli).

Plant exception (HBV): Soya beans and soya products (tofu, tempeh, soya milk).

Protein Complementation

Protein complementation is the practice of combining two or more LBV protein sources at the same meal so that together they provide all eight essential amino acids. The amino acids missing from one food are supplied by the other.

This is especially important for vegetarians and vegans who do not eat animal products. Classic examples include beans on toast (pulses + cereal), rice and lentils (cereal + pulse), and hummus with pitta bread (chickpeas + wheat). As long as a variety of plant proteins are eaten across the day, the body gets everything it needs.

Key Fact

Protein complementation does not mean LBV proteins must be eaten at exactly the same time. Eating a variety of plant proteins across the day will provide all eight EAAs. However, the exam often asks for examples of complementary combinations eaten together.

Protein Alternatives

The specification requires you to know about protein alternatives — products developed to replace or supplement traditional meat and dairy sources. These are increasingly important as more people adopt vegetarian, vegan, or flexitarian diets.

TVP (textured vegetable protein): Made from soya flour that has been processed into a chewy, meat-like texture. It absorbs flavours well and is used in dishes such as chilli, bolognese, and stir-fries. TVP is HBV because it comes from soya.

Tofu: Made by curdling soya milk and pressing the curds into blocks. It comes in firm and silken varieties. Firm tofu can be sliced and stir-fried; silken tofu works in smoothies and desserts. Tofu is HBV and a good source of calcium when set with calcium salts.

Mycoprotein (Quorn™): Made from a mycoprotein — a type of fungus called Fusarium venenatum. It is grown in large fermenters using glucose syrup. Mycoprotein is high in protein and fibre, low in saturated fat, and has a texture similar to chicken. It is HBV.

Soya products: Soya beans are processed into many forms: soya milk, soya mince, soya yoghurt, tempeh (fermented soya), and edamame beans. All are HBV. Soya is one of the 14 major food allergens, so it must be declared on food labels.

Dietary Reference Values

Dietary reference values (DRVs) are guidelines that show how much of a nutrient different groups of people need. For protein, the reference nutrient intake (RNI) for adults is 0.75 g per kilogram of bodyweight per day. So a person weighing 70 kg needs approximately 52.5 g of protein daily.

Some groups need more protein than the standard RNI: growing children and teenagers, pregnant and breastfeeding women, people recovering from illness or surgery, and athletes building muscle. The reference intakes (RIs) shown on food labels use a standard value of 50 g protein per day for an average adult.

Deficiency and Excess

Deficiency: A lack of protein can lead to poor growth in children, slow wound healing, muscle wasting, weakened immunity, and a condition called kwashiorkor (swollen abdomen, thinning hair, skin lesions) — most commonly seen in developing countries where food is scarce. In the UK, protein deficiency is rare but can occur in people with very restricted diets or eating disorders.

Excess: Eating more protein than the body needs is not stored as protein. Excess amino acids are broken down by the liver in a process called deamination. The nitrogen part is converted to urea and excreted by the kidneys. Over long periods, very high protein intakes may put strain on the kidneys and liver. Excess protein can also be converted to fat and stored, contributing to weight gain.

Too little protein: Poor growth, slow healing, muscle wasting, weak immune system, kwashiorkor. Too much protein: Strain on kidneys and liver, excess converted to fat (weight gain), deamination produces urea. A balanced diet provides enough protein without excess.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When an AQA Food Technology question asks you to “explain” something about protein, always link your answer back to the science: name specific amino acids or the HBV/LBV distinction, give food source examples, and explain the consequence for the body. For “discuss” questions worth 8 marks, make sure you cover both sides — for example, the benefits and drawbacks of protein alternatives — and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Protein is made of amino acids — 8 are essential (must come from food). HBV sources (animal + soya) contain all 8; LBV sources (most plants) are missing one or more.
  • Protein complementation means combining LBV sources (e.g. beans on toast) to get all essential amino acids — vital for vegetarians and vegans.
  • Know the four protein alternatives for the exam: TVP, tofu, mycoprotein (Quorn), and soya products — plus the effects of both deficiency and excess.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using protein alternatives such as mycoprotein (Quorn) and tofu instead of meat.

• Lower in saturated fat than red meat, which may reduce risk of heart disease (1)
• Mycoprotein is high in fibre, which aids digestion (1)
• More sustainable — lower carbon footprint and water use than animal farming (1)

Disadvantages may include:

• Taste and texture may not appeal to everyone, especially compared to meat (1)
• Some products are highly processed with added salt, flavourings, or preservatives (1)
• Mycoprotein can cause digestive issues in some people (1)
• May be more expensive than cheaper cuts of meat (1)
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good range of points on both sides with some specific detail but conclusion may be brief.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points but unbalanced or lacking specific detail.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points, one-sided, or mostly generic statements.

lessons.title: Macronutrients: Fats and Carbohydrates
lessons.description: Saturated and unsaturated fats, simple and complex carbohydrates, and dietary fibre.
lessons.content_html:
Introduction to Fats and Carbohydrates

Fats and carbohydrates are two of the three macronutrients. Together with protein, they provide the energy your body needs to function. Both topics frequently appear in exam questions.

Understanding the different types of fats and carbohydrates, where they come from, and what they do in the body is essential for answering both short and extended-response questions confidently.

What Are Fats?

Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient, providing 9 kcal per gram — more than double the energy of protein or carbohydrate (both 4 kcal/g). Fats are also called lipids. The key difference between fats and oils is their state at room temperature: fats are solid (e.g. butter, lard) and oils are liquid (e.g. olive oil, sunflower oil).

Government guidelines recommend that no more than 35% of total energy should come from fat, and saturated fat should be less than 11% of total energy intake.

Key Fact

Fat provides 9 kcal per gram — more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate. Government advice: total fat <35% of energy, saturated fat <11%.

Types of Fat

Fats are classified by their chemical structure — specifically, whether or not their carbon chains contain double bonds between carbon atoms. This determines whether a fat is saturated or unsaturated.

Saturated fat has no double bonds between the carbon atoms in its fatty acid chains. The carbon chain is fully “saturated” with hydrogen atoms. Saturated fats are typically solid at room temperature.

Sources: Fatty meat, butter, lard, hard cheese, cream, cakes, biscuits, pastries, and coconut oil.

Health link: Eating too much saturated fat raises levels of LDL (“bad”) cholesterol in the blood, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD). This is why the government recommends keeping saturated fat below 11% of total energy intake.

Monounsaturated fat has one double bond in its fatty acid chain. It is liquid at room temperature but may solidify when chilled. Sources: Olive oil, rapeseed oil, avocados, almonds, and peanuts.

Polyunsaturated fat has two or more double bonds in its fatty acid chains. It is always liquid at room temperature. Sources: Sunflower oil, corn oil, seeds, walnuts, and oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines).

Health link: Unsaturated fats can help lower LDL cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart disease when they replace saturated fats in the diet. Polyunsaturated fats include essential fatty acids such as omega-3 (found in oily fish) and omega-6 (found in vegetable oils), which the body cannot make itself.

Key Fact — Saturated vs Unsaturated

Saturated: No double bonds, solid at room temperature, raises LDL cholesterol. Monounsaturated: One double bond, liquid at room temperature. Polyunsaturated: Two or more double bonds, liquid at room temperature, includes omega-3 and omega-6.

Functions of Fat

Fat performs several important roles in the body. You need to know these for the exam because questions often ask you to explain why fat is needed, not just what it is.

Energy: Fat is the body’s most concentrated energy source (9 kcal/g). It provides a long-lasting energy reserve. Insulation: A layer of fat beneath the skin (subcutaneous fat) helps maintain body temperature by reducing heat loss. Protection: Fat cushions and protects vital organs such as the kidneys, heart, and liver from physical damage.

Fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble vitamins. This means the body needs dietary fat to absorb and transport them. Without enough fat in the diet, a person could become deficient in these vitamins even if they eat foods that contain them.

What Are Carbohydrates?

Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred and most readily available source of energy, providing 4 kcal per gram. Government guidelines recommend that approximately 50% of total energy should come from carbohydrate, with free sugars making up no more than 5% of total energy.

Carbohydrates are classified into three groups based on their chemical structure: monosaccharides (simple sugars), disaccharides (double sugars), and polysaccharides (complex carbohydrates).

Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates — single sugar molecules that cannot be broken down further. The three you need to know are:

Glucose: Found in fruits, vegetables, and honey. It is the body’s main energy source and circulates in the blood. Fructose: Found naturally in fruits and honey — it is the sweetest natural sugar. Galactose: Found in milk and dairy products. It combines with glucose to form lactose.

Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join together. The three you need to know are:

Sucrose (glucose + fructose): Table sugar — found in sugar cane, sugar beet, and added to many processed foods. Lactose (glucose + galactose): Milk sugar — found naturally in milk and dairy products. Some people are lactose intolerant, meaning they lack the enzyme to digest it. Maltose (glucose + glucose): Malt sugar — found in malted foods, cereals, and produced during digestion of starch.

Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharide units. They take longer to digest, which means they release energy slowly and steadily.

Starch: The main energy-providing polysaccharide in the diet. Found in potatoes, bread, pasta, rice, cereals, and root vegetables. Glycogen: The storage form of glucose in the body, held in the liver and muscles. It is broken down to release glucose when the body needs energy quickly (e.g. during exercise). Dietary fibre (NSP): Found in plant cell walls. Not digested by the body but plays a vital role in keeping the digestive system healthy.

Key Fact — Sugar Classification

Monosaccharides: Glucose, fructose, galactose (single sugars). Disaccharides: Sucrose, lactose, maltose (double sugars). Polysaccharides: Starch, glycogen, dietary fibre (complex, slow-release energy).

Dietary Fibre

Dietary fibre (also called non-starch polysaccharide or NSP) is a type of polysaccharide that the body cannot digest. Despite this, it plays a crucial role in health. The government recommends adults eat 30 g of fibre per day.

Functions of fibre: It adds bulk to food, making you feel full (which helps prevent overeating). It absorbs water and helps move food through the digestive system, preventing constipation. A high-fibre diet is linked to a reduced risk of bowel cancer, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

Sources: Wholegrain bread, brown rice, wholemeal pasta, oats, pulses (lentils, beans, chickpeas), fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. Choosing wholegrain versions of bread, rice, and pasta is one of the easiest ways to increase fibre intake.

Free Sugars

Free sugars are sugars added to food and drink by the manufacturer, cook, or consumer, plus sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and unsweetened fruit juices. They do not include sugars found naturally in whole fruit, vegetables, or milk.

The government recommends that free sugars should make up no more than 5% of total energy intake. Excess free sugar consumption is linked to tooth decay, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. This is why food labels must now show “of which sugars” to help consumers make informed choices.

Key Fact — Fibre and Free Sugars

Adults should aim for 30 g of fibre per day (from wholegrain, fruit, vegetables, and pulses) and limit free sugars to less than 5% of total energy. These two targets work together — choosing wholegrain and whole fruit over refined and sweetened alternatives achieves both.

Deficiency and Excess

Fat deficiency: Too little fat can lead to poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), dry skin, poor temperature regulation, and low energy levels. Fat excess: Too much fat, especially saturated fat, leads to weight gain, obesity, raised cholesterol, and increased risk of coronary heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

Carbohydrate deficiency: Without enough carbohydrate, the body uses protein and fat for energy instead, which can cause tiredness, poor concentration, ketosis, and muscle wasting. Carbohydrate excess: Excess carbohydrate (especially free sugars) is converted to fat and stored, leading to weight gain, obesity, tooth decay, and increased risk of type 2 diabetes.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In AQA Food Technology questions about fats or carbohydrates, always be specific about the type (e.g. saturated vs polyunsaturated, monosaccharide vs polysaccharide). Naming specific food sources and linking them to health effects will push your answer into the higher mark bands. For “discuss” questions, consider both positive roles (energy, insulation, vitamins) and negative effects of excess (CHD, obesity, tooth decay) to show balance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fats provide 9 kcal/g and come in three types: saturated (no double bonds, raises cholesterol), monounsaturated (one double bond), and polyunsaturated (two or more double bonds, includes omega-3 and omega-6).
  • Carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose), and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, fibre) — complex carbs release energy slowly.
  • Government targets: fat <35% of energy (saturated <11%), carbohydrate ~50% of energy (free sugars <5%), fibre 30 g/day from wholegrain sources.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides. Give an example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Monosaccharides are single sugar units / the simplest form of carbohydrate, e.g. glucose, fructose, or galactose (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why the government recommends that adults eat 30 g of dietary fibre per day. Refer to the health benefits of fibre in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough explanation with multiple health benefits clearly linked to fibre intake, using specific examples.
E.g. Dietary fibre adds bulk to food and absorbs water, which helps move food through the digestive system and prevents constipation. Fibre makes you feel full, which helps prevent overeating and supports weight management. A high-fibre diet is associated with a reduced risk of bowel cancer because waste moves through the intestines more quickly, reducing exposure to harmful substances. Fibre also helps lower blood cholesterol and reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes by slowing the release of glucose into the blood. Wholegrain bread, brown rice, pulses, and fruit and vegetables are all good sources.
Mid band (3-4): Sound explanation with some health benefits but limited development or missing specific detail.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about fibre being good for digestion, limited or no specific health benefits named.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the health consequences of eating too much saturated fat and too much free sugar. Refer to specific conditions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-8): Thorough, balanced discussion covering health consequences of both saturated fat excess and free sugar excess with specific conditions named. Reaches a justified conclusion.
Saturated fat excess may include:
• Raises LDL (‘bad’) cholesterol in the blood (1)
• Increases the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke (1)
• Contributes to weight gain and obesity because fat is energy-dense at 9 kcal/g (1)
• Linked to increased risk of type 2 diabetes (1)
Free sugar excess may include:
• Causes tooth decay — bacteria in the mouth feed on sugar and produce acid that erodes enamel (1)
• Leads to weight gain and obesity because excess sugar is converted to fat and stored (1)
• Increases the risk of type 2 diabetes due to repeated blood sugar spikes (1)
• Provides ‘empty calories’ — energy without essential nutrients (1)
Conclusion: Both should be limited — saturated fat below 11% and free sugars below 5% of total energy.
Upper-mid band (5-6): Good range of points on both topics with some specific conditions but conclusion may be brief.
Lower-mid band (3-4): Some valid points but unbalanced or lacking specific health conditions.
Lower band (1-2): Limited points, one-sided, or mostly generic statements.

lessons.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins
lessons.description: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins, their sources, functions, and deficiency diseases.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Vitamins?

Vitamins are micronutrients — the body only needs them in tiny amounts, but without them things go seriously wrong. Unlike macronutrients, vitamins do not provide energy directly, but many are involved in the chemical reactions that release energy from food, as well as controlling vital processes like bone growth, wound healing, and protecting cells from damage.

Vitamins are split into two groups based on how the body absorbs and stores them: fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C). This distinction matters because it affects how the body absorbs them, how they can be lost during cooking, and what happens if you consume too much.

Key Fact

Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) dissolve in fat and are stored in the liver and body fat. Because they are stored, it is possible to consume too much over time. Water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C) dissolve in water and cannot be stored — excess is excreted in urine, so they must be consumed regularly.

Fat-Soluble Vitamins

Fat-soluble vitamins require dietary fat to be absorbed in the small intestine. They are transported in the blood attached to fat molecules and stored in the liver and adipose tissue. Because they are stored, a daily intake is not strictly necessary — but long-term deficiency causes serious health problems.

Vitamin A has three main functions: it is needed for normal vision, particularly seeing in dim light; it supports the immune system by helping the body fight infections; and it keeps skin and mucous membranes healthy, acting as a barrier against bacteria.

Sources: Liver, oily fish, dairy products (butter, cheese, whole milk), eggs, and orange-coloured vegetables such as carrots, sweet potatoes, and butternut squash. The orange colour comes from beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. Dark green leafy vegetables like spinach also contain beta-carotene.

Deficiency: A lack of vitamin A causes night blindness — difficulty seeing in dim or dark conditions. In severe cases, it can lead to complete blindness. Deficiency also weakens the immune system and makes skin dry and rough.

Vitamin D is sometimes called the “sunshine vitamin” because the body can make it when the skin is exposed to sunlight (specifically ultraviolet B radiation). Its main function is to help the body absorb calcium from food, which is essential for building and maintaining strong bones and teeth.

Sources: Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel), eggs, red meat, and fortified foods such as breakfast cereals and margarine. In the UK, sunlight is only strong enough to make vitamin D between April and September, so the government recommends a 10 microgram supplement during autumn and winter.

Deficiency: Without enough vitamin D, the body cannot absorb calcium properly. In children, this causes rickets — soft, weak bones that bow under the body’s weight. In adults, the equivalent condition is called osteomalacia, which causes bone pain and muscle weakness.

Vitamin E is a powerful antioxidant. It protects cell membranes from damage caused by free radicals. Sources include vegetable oils (sunflower, olive), nuts (almonds, hazelnuts), seeds, and avocados.

Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting. Without it, even small cuts would bleed excessively. It is also involved in bone health. Sources include green leafy vegetables (broccoli, spinach, kale, cabbage), vegetable oils, and some fermented foods.

Key Fact

Remember ADEK for the four fat-soluble vitamins. A = vision + immunity. D = calcium absorption + bones. E = antioxidant. K = blood clotting. They all need dietary fat to be absorbed.

Water-Soluble Vitamins: B-Group

The B-group vitamins are a family of water-soluble vitamins that work together in the body. They cannot be stored, so they must be consumed regularly through the diet. Several B vitamins are involved in releasing energy from carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

B1

Thiamin

Helps release energy from carbohydrates. Found in wholegrains, pork, nuts, and fortified cereals. Deficiency causes beriberi (nerve and heart damage).

B2

Riboflavin

Helps release energy from food and supports healthy skin and eyes. Found in milk, eggs, fortified cereals, and mushrooms.

B3

Niacin

Helps release energy from food and supports the nervous system and skin. Found in meat, fish, wheat flour, and eggs.

B9

Folic Acid (Folate)

Essential for cell division and the formation of DNA. Critical during early pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects (e.g. spina bifida). Found in green leafy vegetables, pulses (chickpeas, lentils), fortified bread, and oranges.

B12

Cobalamin

Needed for making red blood cells and maintaining the nervous system. Found only in animal sources: meat, fish, dairy, and eggs. Vegans are at risk of deficiency and should take supplements or eat fortified foods.

Key Fact

Vitamin B12 is found only in animal sources. This means vegans must get it from fortified foods (plant milks, nutritional yeast, breakfast cereals) or supplements. A deficiency causes a type of anaemia (megaloblastic anaemia) where red blood cells are too large and do not function properly.

Water-Soluble Vitamins: Vitamin C

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) has several important functions. It is needed for the formation of collagen, a protein that forms connective tissue in the skin, blood vessels, tendons, and ligaments. This means vitamin C is essential for wound healing — without it, wounds take much longer to repair.

Vitamin C also helps the body absorb iron from plant sources (non-haem iron), so eating vitamin C-rich foods alongside iron-rich foods improves iron uptake. On top of this, vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant, protecting cells from free radical damage.

Sources: Citrus fruits (oranges, lemons, grapefruits), peppers (especially red and green), broccoli, strawberries, blackcurrants, kiwi fruit, tomatoes, and potatoes.

Deficiency: A severe lack of vitamin C causes scurvy — symptoms include bleeding gums, loose teeth, bruising easily, poor wound healing, and joint pain. Historically, scurvy was common among sailors on long voyages with no access to fresh fruit or vegetables.

Cooking & Water-Soluble Vitamin Loss

Because B vitamins and vitamin C dissolve in water, they can easily be lost during food preparation and cooking. This is an important practical point for the exam — you may be asked how to retain vitamins when cooking vegetables.

How they are lost: Boiling vegetables in large amounts of water causes vitamins to leach out into the cooking water, which is then thrown away. Overcooking destroys vitamins through prolonged exposure to heat. Chopping vegetables into very small pieces increases the surface area exposed to water and air, speeding up vitamin loss. Keeping food warm for long periods also reduces vitamin content.

How to minimise loss: Steam vegetables instead of boiling. Use as little water as possible if boiling. Cook for the shortest time necessary. Keep vegetables in large pieces until just before cooking. Serve immediately rather than keeping warm. Use the cooking water for sauces or gravy to retain any leached vitamins.

Antioxidant Vitamins: A, C, and E

Vitamins A, C, and E all have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants protect the body’s cells from damage caused by free radicals — unstable molecules produced during normal metabolism and by environmental factors such as pollution, cigarette smoke, and UV radiation.

Free radicals can damage cell membranes and DNA, contributing to ageing and increasing the risk of diseases such as cancer, heart disease, and cataracts. A diet rich in antioxidant vitamins — from colourful fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds — helps neutralise free radicals and reduce this damage. This is why the government recommends eating at least five portions of fruit and vegetables per day.

Key Fact

The three antioxidant vitamins are A, C, and E (remember: “ACE”). They protect cells from free radical damage. A diet rich in colourful fruits and vegetables provides all three. In the exam, link antioxidants to reduced risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature ageing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering AQA questions about vitamins, always state the specific vitamin, its function, a named food source, and the consequence of deficiency or excess. For example: “Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones. Sources include oily fish and eggs. A deficiency in children causes rickets.” If asked about cooking methods, link your answer to water-soluble vitamin loss and explain how to minimise it (steam, less water, shorter cooking time). For higher-mark questions, always explain the science behind your answer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) need dietary fat for absorption and are stored in the body — key deficiency diseases include night blindness (A), rickets and osteomalacia (D).
  • Water-soluble vitamins (B-group and C) cannot be stored and are easily lost through boiling and overcooking — B12 is only in animal sources (vegans at risk), and vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
  • Vitamins A, C, and E are antioxidants (“ACE”) that protect cells from free radical damage, reducing the risk of cancer, heart disease, and premature ageing.

lessons.title: Micronutrients: Minerals and Water
lessons.description: The six key minerals, their functions and food sources, plus why hydration matters.
lessons.content_html:
Minerals in the Diet

Minerals are micronutrients that your body needs in small amounts. Unlike vitamins, minerals are inorganic — they come from the soil and water rather than from living things. For your AQA exam, you need to know six minerals: calcium, iron, sodium, fluoride, iodine, and phosphorus.

Calcium

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body. It is essential for strong bones and teeth, but it also plays a role in muscle contraction, blood clotting, and nerve function. The RNI for adults is 700 mg per day.

Good sources include milk, cheese, yoghurt, green leafy vegetables (such as broccoli and kale), canned fish with bones (like sardines), and fortified foods such as fortified bread and breakfast cereals.

Key Fact

Calcium deficiency causes rickets in children (soft, weak bones that bend) and osteoporosis in adults (brittle bones that fracture easily). Excess calcium can lead to kidney stones.

Iron

Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen around the body. Without enough iron, your cells do not get the oxygen they need, and you feel tired and weak.

There are two types of dietary iron. Haem iron comes from animal sources such as red meat and liver — the body absorbs it easily. Non-haem iron comes from plant sources such as dark green leafy vegetables, beans, nuts, and fortified cereals — it is harder to absorb. Eating vitamin C alongside non-haem iron (for example, a glass of orange juice with a fortified cereal) significantly improves absorption.

Deficiency: Iron deficiency causes anaemia. Symptoms include tiredness, pale skin, and breathlessness. It is one of the most common nutritional deficiencies in the UK, particularly among teenage girls and women of childbearing age.

Excess: Too much iron can cause constipation, nausea, and in severe cases, liver damage. Iron supplements should only be taken on medical advice.

Sodium

Sodium is essential for maintaining fluid balance in the body. It also helps transmit nerve impulses and supports muscle contraction. Most people get sodium from salt (sodium chloride), processed foods, bread, and cheese.

Key Fact

Adults should consume no more than 6 g of salt per day (about one teaspoon). Excess sodium raises blood pressure, increasing the risk of stroke and heart disease. Deficiency is rare but can cause muscle cramps.

Fluoride, Iodine & Phosphorus

Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and helps prevent dental caries (tooth decay). Sources include fluoridated water, tea, and toothpaste. Many areas in the UK add fluoride to the water supply specifically to reduce tooth decay.

Iodine is needed for the production of thyroid hormones, which control your metabolism. Good sources are seafood, milk, and dairy products. A deficiency causes goitre — a visible swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck.

Phosphorus works alongside calcium to build and maintain strong bones and teeth. It also helps the body release energy from food. Sources include meat, fish, dairy, and cereals. Because it is found in so many foods, deficiency is extremely rare.

Calcium — bones, teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction. Sources: dairy, leafy greens, fortified foods. Deficiency: rickets/osteoporosis.

Iron — haemoglobin (oxygen transport). Sources: red meat, liver, beans, fortified cereals. Deficiency: anaemia.

Sodium — fluid balance, nerve impulses, muscle contraction. Sources: salt, processed foods. Excess: high blood pressure. Max 6 g salt/day.

Fluoride — tooth enamel, prevents dental caries. Sources: fluoridated water, tea, toothpaste.

Iodine — thyroid hormones, metabolism. Sources: seafood, milk, dairy. Deficiency: goitre.

Phosphorus — bones/teeth (with calcium), energy release. Sources: meat, fish, dairy, cereals.

Water & Hydration

Water is not a mineral, but it is essential for life. Every cell, tissue, and organ in your body needs water to function properly. The specification requires you to understand the functions of water, how it is lost, and how much you need each day.

Waste elimination: Water helps the kidneys flush out waste products through urine.

Temperature regulation: When you are hot, your body produces sweat. As sweat evaporates from the skin, it cools you down.

Digestion: Water is needed to break down food and absorb nutrients in the digestive system.

Nutrient transport: Blood, which is mostly water, carries nutrients and oxygen to cells and removes waste.

Chemical reactions: Many chemical processes in the body, including hydrolysis, require water to take place.

Water is lost continuously through urine, sweat, and breathing. The government recommends drinking 6–8 glasses of fluid per day. Water, lower-fat milk, and sugar-free drinks all count towards this. About 20% of your daily water intake comes from food — soups, yoghurts, fruit, and vegetables all contain significant amounts of water. The remaining 80% should come from drinks.

Key Fact

Fruit juice and smoothies count as a maximum of 150 ml per day combined, no matter how much you drink, because of their high sugar content. Drinking too much water can cause hyponatraemia — dangerously low sodium levels in the blood.

Extra fluids are needed during hot weather, physical activity, illness (especially fever, vomiting, or diarrhoea), and pregnancy or breastfeeding. Dehydration causes headaches, fatigue, poor concentration, and dark-coloured urine. In severe cases it can be life-threatening.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In AQA Food Technology, “explain” questions about minerals want you to name the mineral, state its function, give food sources, and describe what happens if someone has too little or too much. Always link your answer to a specific group of people where relevant — for example, iron deficiency is particularly common in teenage girls. For “discuss” questions (8 marks), you need to cover multiple minerals or both sides of an argument, and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Six minerals to know: calcium (bones), iron (haemoglobin), sodium (fluid balance), fluoride (teeth), iodine (thyroid), and phosphorus (bones & energy) — each with specific sources, deficiency diseases, and excess risks.
  • Haem iron from animal sources is absorbed more easily than non-haem iron from plants; vitamin C improves non-haem iron absorption.
  • Aim for 6–8 glasses of fluid per day. Water supports waste removal, temperature control, digestion, nutrient transport, and chemical reactions in the body.

lessons.title: The Eatwell Guide and Balanced Diets
lessons.description: The five food groups of the Eatwell Guide, 8 tips for healthier eating, and adapting diets for different needs.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the Eatwell Guide?

The Eatwell Guide is the UK government’s official healthy eating model. It shows the proportions in which different food groups should be eaten over the course of a day or more. The guide is suitable for most people aged 2 and over, and it applies to people of all ethnic backgrounds and body weights.

The Eatwell Guide is shaped like a plate, divided into five food groups of different sizes. The size of each segment shows how much of your overall diet should come from that group. It does not mean every single meal must look like the plate — it represents what you eat across a whole day.

Key Fact

The Eatwell Guide comprises five main food groups. It shows the proportions of each group needed for a balanced diet and is suitable for most people over 2 years of age. The proportions are representative of food eaten over a day or more, not a single meal.

The Five Food Groups

This group should make up just over a third of the food eaten each day. The recommendation is to eat at least five portions of a variety each day. Sources include fresh, frozen, canned, dried, or juiced fruit and vegetables.

A single portion is around 80g (roughly three heaped tablespoons). However, 30g of dried fruit or a 150ml glass of fruit juice or smoothie can only count as a maximum of one portion per day, because drying and juicing concentrates the sugars and removes fibre.

Starchy carbohydrates should form the base of meals and make up just over a third of the diet. These foods provide energy, fibre, B vitamins, and minerals.

The guidance is to choose higher-fibre, wholegrain varieties where possible. Wholegrain options include wholemeal bread, brown rice, and wholewheat pasta. These release energy more slowly and contain more dietary fibre than their refined equivalents.

Dairy products such as milk, cheese, and yoghurt are good sources of protein, vitamins, and an important source of calcium, which helps to keep bones strong. The advice is to choose lower-fat and lower-sugar products where possible.

Alternatives include calcium-fortified soya, oat, or almond drinks. These are particularly important for people who follow a vegan diet or who have lactose intolerance.

This group provides protein, vitamins, and minerals. The recommendation is to aim for at least two portions of fish per week, including one portion of oily fish (such as salmon, mackerel, or sardines). Oily fish is rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which help to protect the heart.

People who eat more than 90g per day of red or processed meat should cut down to no more than 70g per day. Beans and pulses are excellent alternatives because they are high in fibre, low in fat, and count towards the 5-a-day target.

Unsaturated fats are healthier fats, usually from plant sources and in liquid form as oil — for example, olive oil or rapeseed oil. These should be used in small amounts.

Generally, people are eating too much saturated fat and need to reduce their consumption. Saturated fats are found in butter, lard, cheese, cakes, biscuits, and fatty cuts of meat.

Foods High in Fat, Salt and Sugar

Products such as chocolate, cakes, biscuits, full-sugar soft drinks, butter, and ice cream are high in fat, sugar, and energy. These foods are not needed in the diet. If they are included, they should be consumed infrequently and in small amounts. They sit outside the main five food groups on the Eatwell Guide.

Composite and Combination Foods

Much of the food people eat is in the form of dishes or meals made from more than one food group. These are called composite foods (or combination foods). Examples include pizza, casseroles, spaghetti bolognese, lasagne, and sandwiches.

For example, a lasagne contains: pasta sheets (starchy carbohydrates), onions, garlic and chopped tomatoes (fruit and vegetables), lean minced meat (protein), cheese sauce made with milk and cheese (dairy), and olive oil used to cook the mince (oils and spreads). Being able to identify which food group each ingredient belongs to is a key exam skill.

Key Fact

A composite food contains ingredients from more than one food group. In the exam, you may be asked to break down a dish into its Eatwell Guide components — for example, identifying the starchy carbohydrate, protein, dairy, fruit and vegetable, and oil elements in a recipe.

The 8 Tips for Healthier Eating

The government provides eight practical tips that cover the basics of healthy eating:

Tip 1

Base Your Meals on Starchy Carbohydrates

Starchy foods should make up just over a third of everything you eat. Choose wholegrain varieties for extra fibre.

Tip 2

Eat Lots of Fruit and Veg

Aim for at least 5 portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables every day. Fresh, frozen, canned, dried, and juiced all count.

Tip 3

Eat More Fish

Aim for at least 2 portions of fish a week, including 1 portion of oily fish such as salmon or mackerel.

Tip 4

Cut Down on Saturated Fat and Sugar

Too much saturated fat raises blood cholesterol. Too much sugar causes tooth decay and weight gain. Check food labels to make informed choices.

Tip 5

Eat Less Salt

Adults should eat no more than 6g of salt per day. Too much salt raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart disease and stroke.

Tip 6

Get Active and Be a Healthy Weight

Regular physical activity helps maintain a healthy weight and reduces the risk of diet-related diseases.

Tip 7

Don’t Get Thirsty

Aim for 6–8 glasses of fluid every day. Water, lower-fat milk, and sugar-free drinks all count. Limit fruit juice and smoothies to a combined total of 150ml per day.

Tip 8

Don’t Skip Breakfast

A healthy breakfast provides energy and some of the vitamins and minerals needed for good health. Wholegrain cereals with fruit are a nutritious choice.

Hydration

Hydration means replacing the water your body loses throughout the day. The recommendation is to drink 6–8 glasses of fluid every day. Water, lower-fat milk, and sugar-free drinks including tea and coffee all count towards this total.

Fruit juice and smoothies also count, but they should be limited to no more than a combined total of 150ml per day because of their high sugar content. Staying hydrated helps concentration, digestion, and kidney function.

Dietary Fibre

Dietary fibre is a type of carbohydrate found in plant foods. Good sources include wholegrain cereals and cereal products, oats, beans, lentils, fruit, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. The recommended average intake is 30g per day for adults.

Dietary fibre helps to reduce the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers. It also helps with weight control, bulks up stools, prevents constipation, and improves gut health.

Key Fact

Adults need 30g of dietary fibre per day. Good sources include wholegrain cereals, oats, beans, lentils, fruit, vegetables, nuts, and seeds. Fibre reduces the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers, and helps prevent constipation.

Adapting Diets for Different Life Stages

Nutritional needs change throughout life. The Eatwell Guide principles apply to everyone aged 2 and over, but the amounts and emphasis differ by life stage.

Children (2–11 years): Need energy-dense foods for growth and development. Require calcium and vitamin D for strong bones and teeth. Smaller portions than adults, but meals should still follow the Eatwell Guide proportions. Limit sugary snacks and drinks.

Teenagers (12–18 years): High energy needs due to rapid growth spurts. Extra iron is important, especially for girls after the onset of menstruation. Calcium is critical as bones are still developing. Protein is needed for muscle growth.

Adults (19–64 years): Energy needs depend on activity level and body size. A balanced diet following the Eatwell Guide helps maintain a healthy weight and reduce the risk of diet-related diseases such as type 2 diabetes and coronary heart disease.

Elderly (65+ years): Energy needs decrease as activity levels drop, but nutrient needs remain high. Calcium and vitamin D are especially important to prevent osteoporosis. Fibre helps with digestion. Smaller, nutrient-dense meals are recommended.

Adapting Diets for Dietary Groups

Some people need to modify the Eatwell Guide to suit their dietary requirements, whether for ethical, religious, health, or medical reasons.

Vegetarian: Excludes meat and fish but includes dairy and eggs. Protein can come from beans, pulses, eggs, cheese, tofu, and Quorn. Protein complementation — combining different plant proteins at the same meal — ensures all essential amino acids are consumed.

Vegan: Excludes all animal products including dairy, eggs, and honey. Alternative calcium sources include fortified plant milks, tofu, and green leafy vegetables. Vitamin B12 must come from fortified foods or supplements as it is only found naturally in animal products.

Coeliac disease: An autoimmune condition triggered by gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. People with coeliac disease must follow a strict gluten-free diet. Alternatives include rice, potatoes, corn, and gluten-free flour blends.

Lactose intolerant: People who cannot digest lactose, the sugar found in milk, must avoid or limit dairy products. Alternatives include lactose-free milk, calcium-fortified plant milks, and hard cheeses (which are naturally lower in lactose).

High-fibre diet: Recommended for people at risk of constipation, bowel disease, or heart disease. Increase wholegrain cereals, beans, lentils, fruit, and vegetables. The target is 30g of fibre per day for adults.

Portion Size and Costing

Understanding portion size helps people follow the Eatwell Guide without overeating. For example, a portion of fruit or vegetables is about 80g, a portion of meat or fish is roughly the size of a deck of cards, and a portion of cheese is about 30g (matchbox-sized).

When planning meals, costing is also important. Dried pulses and frozen vegetables are often cheaper than fresh alternatives and can help families eat healthily on a budget. Batch cooking and using seasonal produce are practical strategies that reduce food costs while following the Eatwell Guide principles.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In the exam, you may be asked to plan a balanced meal or explain how a diet could be improved using the Eatwell Guide. Always name the specific food groups and give practical food examples rather than vague statements. For ‘explain’ questions, state the nutritional benefit — for example, “switching to wholegrain bread increases dietary fibre intake, which helps prevent constipation and reduces the risk of heart disease.” For ‘discuss’ questions, consider both sides and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of five food groups needed for a balanced diet — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates should each make up about a third of your plate.
  • The 8 tips for healthier eating provide practical guidance including eating 5 portions of fruit and veg daily, limiting salt to 6g per day, drinking 6–8 glasses of fluid, and choosing wholegrain and unsaturated fat options.
  • Diets must be adapted for different life stages (children, teenagers, adults, elderly) and dietary groups (vegetarian, vegan, coeliac, lactose intolerant), while still following the Eatwell Guide principles.

lessons.title: Energy Needs and Nutritional Analysis
lessons.description: BMR, PAL, energy balance, recommended nutrient intakes, and using nutritional analysis software.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Energy?

Your body needs energy for everything it does — from breathing and pumping blood to walking and exercising. This energy comes from the food and drink you consume. The amount of energy a person needs depends on their age, gender, body size, muscle mass, and how active they are.

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is the amount of energy your body needs just to stay alive when you are completely at rest. It covers essential functions like breathing, keeping your heart beating, maintaining body temperature, and repairing cells. BMR accounts for the largest portion of your daily energy use — typically 60–75% of total energy expenditure.

Age: BMR decreases as you get older because muscle mass naturally declines with age. Younger people have a higher BMR because their bodies are still growing and repairing cells rapidly.

Gender: Males generally have a higher BMR than females because they tend to have more muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active — it burns energy even at rest.

Body size: A larger body has more cells to maintain, so taller or heavier people typically have a higher BMR than smaller people.

Muscle mass: The more muscle you have, the higher your BMR. This is why athletes and people who exercise regularly burn more energy at rest than sedentary individuals.

Key Fact

BMR is the energy needed for basic functions at complete rest. It is affected by four main factors: age, gender, body size, and muscle mass. A younger, larger, more muscular male will generally have the highest BMR.

Physical Activity Level (PAL)

Physical Activity Level (PAL) is a value that reflects how active a person is during the day. A sedentary office worker has a low PAL (around 1.4), while an athlete or manual labourer has a high PAL (around 2.0 or more). The more active you are, the higher your PAL.

Sedentary (PAL 1.4): Little or no exercise, desk-based work. Examples include office workers or students who do not take part in sport.

Moderately active (PAL 1.6–1.7): Some regular exercise or a job that involves standing and walking. Examples include teachers or shop workers who also exercise a few times a week.

Very active (PAL 1.9–2.0+): Daily vigorous exercise or a physically demanding job. Examples include professional athletes, builders, or farmers.

Calculating Total Energy Needs

To work out how much energy a person needs each day, you multiply their BMR by their PAL:

Key Fact

Total daily energy requirement = BMR × PAL

For example, if a woman has a BMR of 1,400 kcal and a PAL of 1.6 (moderately active), her total daily energy need is 1,400 × 1.6 = 2,240 kcal per day.

Energy Balance

Energy balance is the relationship between the energy you take in from food and the energy your body uses. When energy in equals energy out, your weight stays stable. When they are not equal, your weight changes.

Energy in = Energy out (balanced): Weight stays the same. The person is eating exactly as much energy as they are using. This is the ideal for maintaining a healthy weight.

Energy in > Energy out (surplus): The excess energy is stored as body fat, leading to weight gain. Over time, this can contribute to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and some cancers.

Energy in < Energy out (deficit): The body uses its stored fat for energy, leading to weight loss. If prolonged, this can cause malnutrition, fatigue, a weakened immune system, and in children it can slow growth and development.

Energy Values of Macronutrients

Different macronutrients provide different amounts of energy per gram. Knowing these values is essential for nutritional analysis and for exam calculations.

4 kcal/g

Protein

Provides 4 kilocalories per gram. Protein is primarily used for growth and repair, but the body can use it for energy when carbohydrate and fat stores are low.

4 kcal/g

Carbohydrate

Provides 4 kilocalories per gram. Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred source of energy, especially for the brain and during exercise.

9 kcal/g

Fat

Provides 9 kilocalories per gram — more than double the energy of protein or carbohydrate. Fat is a concentrated energy source and is stored in the body for use when needed.

7 kcal/g

Alcohol

Provides 7 kilocalories per gram. Alcohol is not a nutrient and has no nutritional benefit, but it does contribute to energy intake.

Key Fact

Energy values you must know: protein = 4 kcal/g, carbohydrate = 4 kcal/g, fat = 9 kcal/g, alcohol = 7 kcal/g. Fat provides more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate gram for gram.

Recommended Macronutrient Proportions

The UK government publishes dietary recommendations for how much of each macronutrient should make up a person’s total energy intake. Following these helps reduce the risk of diet-related diseases.

Protein (~15% of total energy): Supports growth, repair, and maintenance of body tissues. Found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, and nuts.

Fat (no more than 35% of total energy): Provides essential fatty acids and carries fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Within this, saturated fat should be limited to no more than 11% of total energy to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Carbohydrate (~50% of total energy): The body’s preferred energy source. Of this 50%, around 45% should come from starchy carbohydrates (bread, pasta, rice, potatoes). Free sugars should make up no more than 5% of total energy — about 30g per day for adults.

Nutritional Analysis

Nutritional analysis is the process of working out the nutrient and energy content of a food product or meal. It helps food manufacturers, chefs, and individuals understand what they are eating and whether a dish meets dietary guidelines.

Food composition tables: Published tables such as McCance and Widdowson’s The Composition of Foods list the nutrient content of hundreds of foods per 100g. You look up each ingredient, calculate the amounts used in your recipe, and add them together. This manual method is accurate but time-consuming.

Nutritional analysis software: Programs like Nutritics or MyFitnessPal allow you to enter a recipe and instantly see a full nutritional breakdown. The software compares results against reference intakes and can highlight where a dish is too high in fat, sugar, or salt, or too low in fibre or vitamins.

Food labels: Packaged foods display nutritional information per 100g and per portion. Traffic light labels use red, amber, and green to show whether levels of fat, saturated fat, sugar, and salt are high, medium, or low.

Using Nutritional Analysis to Plan and Modify Dishes

In the exam, you may be asked how nutritional analysis can help you plan, make, or modify a dish. The key idea is that once you know the nutritional profile of a recipe, you can adjust ingredients to make it healthier or to meet a specific dietary need.

Reducing fat: Swap butter for a lower-fat spread, grill instead of fry, use semi-skimmed milk instead of whole milk, or trim visible fat from meat.

Reducing sugar: Use fruit purée to sweeten a cake instead of sugar, reduce the amount of sugar in a recipe by one-third, or choose tinned fruit in juice rather than syrup.

Increasing fibre: Use wholemeal flour instead of white flour, add vegetables or pulses to a sauce or stew, or serve brown rice instead of white rice.

Increasing vitamins and minerals: Add extra vegetables, choose fortified cereals, or include a side salad to boost micronutrient content.

Key Fact

In the exam, always justify modifications using nutritional data. For example: “The analysis showed the dish was high in saturated fat (22g per serving), so I swapped butter for olive oil to reduce it to 8g, bringing the fat content below the 35% guideline.”
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on energy needs, always state the formula: Total energy = BMR × PAL and show your working with correct units (kcal). If asked to explain why two people have different energy needs, compare their age, gender, body size, and activity level — give a reason for each factor, not just a list. For nutritional analysis questions, name a specific method (food tables or software) and explain how the results would be used to improve a dish. Strong answers show precise nutritional data, not vague suggestions like “make it healthier.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Total daily energy needs are calculated by multiplying BMR (energy at rest) by PAL (activity level). Key factors affecting BMR are age, gender, body size, and muscle mass.
  • Energy balance means energy in equals energy out — a surplus causes weight gain, a deficit causes weight loss. Recommended proportions: protein ~15%, fat ≤35%, carbohydrate ~50% (free sugars max 5%).
  • Nutritional analysis using food tables or software allows you to assess and modify dishes to meet dietary guidelines and specific nutritional needs.

• The boy is likely to be larger in body size, which also increases BMR (1).

To restore balance: reduce portion sizes, choose lower-fat cooking methods (grilling instead of frying), cut down on free sugars and high-fat snacks, increase fruit, vegetable, and wholegrain intake, and increase physical activity to raise PAL.

• Carbohydrate (50%, mostly starchy): the body’s preferred energy source. Starchy carbohydrates release energy slowly, helping to maintain blood sugar levels. Free sugars (max 5%) should be limited because they contribute to tooth decay, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.
• Following these proportions ensures a balanced diet that meets energy needs without excess, reducing the risk of diet-related diseases.

lessons.title: Diet-Related Health Risks
lessons.description: Obesity, CHD, bone diseases, dental decay, anaemia and type 2 diabetes linked to poor diet.
lessons.content_html:
Overview

A poor diet does not just affect your weight — it can cause serious, long-term health conditions that affect the heart, bones, teeth, blood and the body's ability to manage blood sugar. This lesson focuses on six diet-related health risks: obesity, coronary heart disease (CHD), bone diseases (rickets and osteoporosis), dental decay, iron deficiency anaemia and type 2 diabetes.

You need to understand the cause of each condition, the dietary factors that contribute to it, and the groups most at risk. Link specific nutrients to specific conditions with precision.

Obesity

Obesity occurs when a person's BMI reaches 30 or above. It is caused by a sustained energy imbalance — when energy intake from food consistently exceeds the energy the body uses through basal metabolic rate and physical activity. The excess energy is stored as body fat.

Obesity significantly increases the risk of several serious conditions:

  • Type 2 diabetes — excess body fat makes cells resistant to insulin
  • Coronary heart disease (CHD) — obesity raises blood cholesterol and blood pressure
  • Certain cancers — including bowel, breast and kidney cancer
  • Joint problems — excess weight puts strain on weight-bearing joints such as knees and hips, increasing the risk of osteoarthritis
Key Fact

Obesity is defined as a BMI of 30 or above. It is caused by energy in exceeding energy out over a sustained period. It increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, CHD, certain cancers and joint problems. Prevention focuses on balancing energy intake with physical activity.

Coronary Heart Disease (CHD)

Coronary heart disease occurs when fatty deposits build up inside the coronary arteries — the blood vessels that supply the heart muscle with oxygen. Over time, these deposits narrow the arteries, restricting blood flow. If an artery becomes completely blocked, it causes a heart attack.

Two dietary factors are particularly important:

A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol levels. When there is too much cholesterol in the blood, it is deposited on the walls of arteries, forming fatty plaques. These plaques narrow the arteries and reduce blood flow to the heart. Saturated fat is found in butter, cheese, fatty cuts of meat, cakes, biscuits and palm oil.

To reduce the risk: replace saturated fats with unsaturated fats (such as olive oil and rapeseed oil), eat oily fish twice a week, and increase intake of soluble fibre from oats, beans and lentils — which helps to lower cholesterol.

A diet high in salt causes the body to retain water, which increases blood volume and raises blood pressure. High blood pressure (hypertension) damages the walls of arteries and makes it easier for fatty deposits to accumulate. Adults should consume no more than 6g of salt per day.

To reduce salt intake: use herbs and spices for flavour instead of salt, avoid processed foods (which contain hidden salt), and check food labels for sodium content. Around 75% of the salt people eat comes from processed foods rather than salt added at the table.

Key Fact — CHD Pathway

High saturated fat → raised blood cholesterol → fatty deposits in artery walls → narrowed arteries → reduced blood flow → heart attack. High salt → water retention → raised blood pressure → damaged artery walls → increased risk of CHD and stroke.

Bone Diseases: Rickets and Osteoporosis

Two important bone conditions are linked to dietary deficiencies:

Rickets is a childhood condition caused by a lack of vitamin D and/or calcium. Without enough of these nutrients, bones cannot mineralise properly and remain soft and weak. This can cause bowed legs, bone pain and poor growth.

Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from food. The body makes vitamin D when skin is exposed to sunlight, but dietary sources are also important — especially oily fish, eggs, fortified cereals and fortified margarine. Children who spend little time outdoors, or who have darker skin (which produces less vitamin D from sunlight), are at greater risk.

Osteoporosis is a condition that mainly affects elderly people, particularly post-menopausal women. Bones gradually lose density and become fragile and brittle, making fractures much more likely — especially in the hip, wrist and spine.

A lifetime of insufficient calcium and vitamin D intake contributes to osteoporosis. Calcium-rich foods include milk, cheese, yoghurt, canned fish with bones (sardines), and green leafy vegetables (broccoli, kale). Weight-bearing exercise also helps maintain bone density.

Dental Decay

Dental decay (also called dental caries or tooth decay) occurs when bacteria in the mouth feed on sugars from food and drink. As the bacteria break down the sugars, they produce acid. This acid attacks the hard outer layer of the tooth — the enamel — gradually dissolving it. Over time, this creates holes (cavities) in the teeth.

The more frequently sugary foods and drinks are consumed, the more often the teeth are under acid attack. Sticky, sugary foods are particularly harmful because they cling to the teeth for longer. The risk increases with the frequency of sugar intake, not just the total amount.

Key Fact

The pathway of dental decay: sugars in food → bacteria feed on sugars → acid produced → enamel dissolves → cavities form. It is the frequency of sugar consumption that matters most, not just the quantity. Limiting sugary snacks between meals reduces the number of acid attacks on teeth.

Iron Deficiency Anaemia

Iron deficiency anaemia occurs when the body does not have enough iron to produce adequate amounts of haemoglobin — the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. Without enough haemoglobin, cells do not receive sufficient oxygen, leading to tiredness, pale skin, breathlessness and difficulty concentrating.

Teenage girls are at particular risk because they lose iron through menstruation. If their diet does not replace this lost iron, anaemia can develop. Girls aged 11–18 need 14.8mg of iron per day.

Vegetarians and vegans are also at increased risk because the most easily absorbed form of iron (haem iron) comes from animal sources such as red meat, liver and kidney. Plant-based iron (non-haem iron) from spinach, lentils, beans and fortified cereals is less readily absorbed by the body.

Vitamin C aids iron absorption. Eating vitamin C-rich foods (such as oranges, peppers or tomatoes) at the same meal as iron-rich foods significantly increases the amount of non-haem iron the body absorbs. This is especially important for vegetarians and vegans.

Key Fact — Iron Absorption

There are two forms of dietary iron: haem iron (from animal sources — easily absorbed) and non-haem iron (from plant sources — less easily absorbed). Consuming vitamin C alongside non-haem iron significantly improves absorption. Tea and coffee can reduce iron absorption.

Type 2 Diabetes

Type 2 diabetes is a condition where the body's cells stop responding properly to insulin — the hormone that controls blood sugar levels. This is called insulin resistance. As a result, glucose remains in the blood instead of entering cells for energy, causing blood sugar levels to rise dangerously.

Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to:

  • Obesity — excess body fat, particularly around the abdomen, increases insulin resistance
  • A diet high in sugar and refined carbohydrates — causes repeated blood sugar spikes that strain the body's insulin response over time
  • Physical inactivity — exercise helps cells use glucose more effectively

Type 2 diabetes can be managed and sometimes reversed through dietary changes, weight loss and regular exercise. Key dietary strategies include reducing sugar and refined carbohydrate intake, eating more wholegrain foods (which release energy slowly), increasing fibre intake, and maintaining a healthy weight through energy balance.

Key Fact

Type 2 diabetes is caused by insulin resistance — the body's cells stop responding to insulin, so blood sugar stays high. It is strongly linked to obesity, high sugar diets and inactivity. Management includes diet modification, weight loss and exercise.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on diet-related health risks, always use the correct pathway — for example, “high saturated fat → raised blood cholesterol → fatty deposits in arteries → narrowed arteries → CHD.” Examiners reward precise chains of cause and effect, not vague statements like “eating too much fat is bad for you.” If asked to ‘evaluate’ or ‘discuss,’ consider both the dietary cause and how it can be managed or prevented. Always name specific nutrients, not just food groups.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Obesity (BMI ≥30) is caused by energy in exceeding energy out, increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes, CHD, cancers and joint problems. CHD results from high saturated fat (raising cholesterol) and high salt (raising blood pressure).
  • Rickets (children, vitamin D/calcium deficiency, soft bones) and osteoporosis (elderly, brittle bones) are both prevented by adequate calcium and vitamin D. Dental decay is caused by frequent sugar consumption feeding bacteria that produce enamel-destroying acid.
  • Iron deficiency anaemia results from insufficient iron for haemoglobin production — teenage girls and vegetarians are most at risk, and vitamin C aids absorption. Type 2 diabetes is linked to obesity and high sugar intake, causing insulin resistance.

practice_questions.text: A teenager is eating a diet high in sugary snacks between meals and drinking several cans of fizzy drink each day. practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (up to 12 marks + 4 spelling/grammar):

Short-term effects:
• Dental decay — frequent sugar intake feeds bacteria that produce acid, attacking tooth enamel and causing cavities (1–2).
• Energy imbalance — excess sugar provides energy beyond needs, leading to weight gain (1).
• Blood sugar spikes — refined sugars cause rapid rises and falls in blood glucose, leading to energy crashes and poor concentration (1).

Long-term effects:
• Obesity — sustained energy surplus leads to BMI of 30+, increasing risk of CHD, cancers and joint problems (1–2).
• Type 2 diabetes — repeated blood sugar spikes strain insulin response; obesity increases insulin resistance (1–2).
• Coronary heart disease — obesity raises cholesterol and blood pressure (1).

Dietary recommendations:
• Replace fizzy drinks with water, milk or sugar-free alternatives (1).
• Swap sugary snacks for fruit, nuts or wholegrain options (1).
• Reduce frequency of sugar consumption rather than just total amount, to limit acid attacks on teeth (1).
• Follow the Eatwell Guide — free sugars should be no more than 5% of total energy (about 30g per day) (1).
• Include regular meals with complex carbohydrates for steady energy release (1).
